prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, clearly bounded invention. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift from the trapping field, so thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated simultaneously in the Lamb-Dicke regime. Ye's group then showed what that architecture can deliver: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, a millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample, and the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) physics that had to be controlled. Several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) now agree at that level, so the result is independently confirmed. It feeds relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter searches, and the coming redefinition of the second. The discovery-or-invention criterion is met cleanly, the credit fits two names, and the attribution fits the physics: a proposal and first realization, then the performance breakthrough. A reader of the 2005 comb citation would see this as a distinct step: the comb made optical frequencies countable, and the lattice clock is what is now counted with them.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges of the clock field. Single-ion optical clocks (Wineland's group and others) reached comparable or better systematic uncertainty by a different route. The French (Lemonde, Le Targat) and PTB/NIST lattice work contributed to the early demonstrations. A narrowly framed lattice-clock citation could look as if it favours the neutral-atom route and leaves out the ion-clock lineage. The atomic physics is also close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, so a committee could judge the novelty claim incremental in kind. Finally, the SI redefinition has not happened, so some colleagues may prefer to wait for it. I weigh these as framing issues rather than reasons against the science, and I rank the clock first knowing that my own expertise is closest to it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first for the same reasons I do (magic wavelength, Lamb-Dicke trapping, 1e-18 agreement, geodesy), and notes that ion clocks and the frequency comb sit nearby.
responses.response: I agree on the science, and I think we should be equally frank that two of the first-place votes on this list come from atomic-physics members. That is a reason to test the case against colleagues from other subfields, not to assume it is settled. I would resist his second choice, B010, as a companion. Cirac-Zoller, Blatt and the lattice-simulation strand are really two achievements, and the three-name limit forces the committee to leave out Bloch or Zoller-and-Bloch type claims. That would reopen the attribution disputes that make B015 attractive. I prefer the lattice clock as a stand-alone prize with its two names.

responses.point: Danielsson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a theory prediction followed by a nature-led experimental surprise, and ranks the lattice clock fourth.
responses.response: I take the discovery-led argument seriously, and a prediction followed by an unexpected result is a strong story. My difficulty is maturity: the origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated states is still disputed, and the credit leaves out the early experimental work and the 2010 prediction lineage that other members flagged. By contrast, lattice clocks have been confirmed for a decade with agreed uncertainties, and the claim does not depend on a mechanism that is still unresolved. I would keep B006 as an alternative for a later year, not as this year's lead, but I accept that it has the broadest support in the opening rankings.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks KPZ universality first as a conceptually clean far-from-equilibrium theory with experimental confirmation of Tracy-Widom statistics, and puts the lattice clock second.
responses.response: KPZ is a beautiful case and I do not dispute the physics. My concern is attribution. Kardar and Zhang are clear for the equation, but the exact-solution results that tied it to random-matrix statistics came from mathematical physicists not in the credit, so the 'discovery' is split between an equation and its later solution. Only one member ranked it, and I am not persuaded it can carry a prize this year. I am glad he rates B015 second, and I would ask him whether the statistical-mechanics side of the committee sees a measurement prize as too narrow compared with a theory prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a decisive instrument-plus-discovery case that opened neutrino astronomy, with the confirmed diffuse flux and the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results.
responses.response: IceCube is a real discovery of nature and the diffuse-flux confirmation is solid. I qualify it on two points: source identification is still partial, and a collaboration of hundreds makes the Halzen, Karle, Spiering split arbitrary in a way the lattice-clock pair is not. I would not oppose it as a later prize, but on the evidence in front of us I find the clock's attribution and confirmation cleaner.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat single-ion optical clocks as part of the same achievement, which would reopen the attribution question and might need a different configuration.
How much weight the redefinition of the SI second should carry; it has not happened, and I do not know if colleagues regard that as a precondition.
B024 (circuit QED) is my second choice but sits close to the 2025 circuit prize, and I have not resolved whether that is a strength or a reason to wait.
I rely on my recollection of the clock literature and have not verified specific uncertainty records.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B015 first, and the field is my own subfield of atomic physics and precision spectroscopy. My profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, so no specific recusal is apparent for B015. For B024 I note that I have documented collaborations at ETH Zurich (with Ursula Keller's group, not Wallraff's), a proximity I disclose without inferring any relationship. For B010 and the attosecond-related strands, my documented collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund group is not relevant to the shortlisted ballots here.
